'''Richard A. Leibler''' ({{IPAc-en|l|ai|b|l|@r}};<ref>{{Cite tweet |user=ProbFact |number=369161957099569153 |title="The ‘ei’ in Leibler is pronounced the same as in heist." -- David MacKay re Richard Leibler of Kullback-Leibler divergence.}}</ref> March 18, 1914{{snd}}October 25, 2003) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[cryptanalyst]]. Richard Leibler was born in March 1914. He received his A.M. in mathematics from [[Northwestern University]] and his Ph.D. from the [[University of Illinois]] in 1939. While working at the [[National Security Agency]], he and [[Solomon Kullback]] formulated the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]],<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Kullback |first1=S. |authorlink1=Solomon Kullback
 |last2=Leibler |first2=R.A. |authorlink2=Richard Leibler
 |year = 1951
 |title = On information and sufficiency
 |journal = [[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]]
 |volume = 22 |issue=1
 |pages=79–86
 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729694 |mr=39968
|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journalArticle/Download?urlId=10.1214%2Faoms%2F1177729694}}</ref> a measure of similarity between probability distributions which has found important applications in [[information theory]] and [[cryptology]]. Leibler is also credited by the NSA as having opened up "new methods of attack" in the celebrated [[Venona project|VENONA]] code-breaking project during 1949-1950;<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nsa.gov/about/_files/cryptologic_heritage/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf |title=Robert Benson, ''The Venona Story'' NSA publications |access-date=2015-02-12 |archive-date=2014-10-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141027140153/https://www.nsa.gov/about/_files/cryptologic_heritage/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> this may be a reference to his joint paper with Kullback, which was published in the open literature in 1951 and was immediately noted by Soviet cryptologists.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=1gb5QxSXUTcC&dq=Solomon+Kullback+Venona&pg=PA433 Suhov, Y and Kelbert, M ''Probability and Statistics by Example'' vol 2 (CUP, 2008) p433 ]</ref>

He was director of the [[Institute for Defense Analyses#Center for Communications and Computing|Communications Research Division at the Institute for Defense Analyses]] from 1962 to 1977, during which he was the boss of [[Jim Simons]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zuckerman |first=Gregory |title=The man who solved the market |date=2019 |publisher=Portfolio / Penguin |isbn=978-0-7352-1798-0 |location=New York, NY |pages=26}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[NSA Hall of Honor]] for his efforts against the VENONA code.<ref>{{Citation |newspaper=NSA History Today|date=17 June 2014|title=Gene Grabeel|accessdate=2015-05-15|url=http://cryptome.org/2015/05/nsa-history-today-2011-15.pdf|pages=30}}</ref>
